questions.question: EC2 vs ECS vs EKS vs Fargate vs Lambda — which AWS compute and when?
questions.title: AWS Compute Compared: EC2, ECS, EKS, Fargate, Lambda, App Runner
questions.direct_answer: Pick by workload shape, ops appetite, and cost model. **Lambda** for event-driven, short, spiky workloads (request-response under 15min, no warm-state). **App Runner / Fargate** for stateless containers without managing servers. **ECS on EC2** when you want container orchestration with control over instances. **EKS** when you need Kubernetes ecosystem (multi-cloud portability, complex deployments). **EC2** when you need full OS control, GPU/specialized hardware, or run software that doesn't containerize cleanly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical compute selection across workload patterns and operational maturity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Defaulting to EKS for everything (operational complexity), or sticking with EC2 because 'it's how we've always done it' when Fargate or Lambda would be simpler
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the cost crossover (Lambda gets expensive past certain RPS), cold start trade-offs, vendor lock-in (Lambda is most locked-in), Spot vs On-Demand, and Graviton (ARM) for cost savings

sections.title: AWS Compute Is a Spectrum from Most-Managed to Most-Control
sections.content:
AWS gives you six main compute options. The right one depends on three axes:
- **Workload shape**: long-running service vs event-driven; stateful vs stateless; predictable vs spiky
- **Operational appetite**: do you want to manage servers, or pay AWS to manage them for you?
- **Cost model**: pay-per-request (Lambda) vs pay-per-second instance time (Fargate, EC2) vs pay-per-instance-hour (EC2 Reserved/Spot)

The spectrum from most-managed to most-control:

**Lambda** — fully managed, runs your code on demand; you provide a function; AWS provides everything else (servers, scaling, patching). Pay per invocation + execution time. Limits: 15-minute max execution, 10GB memory, cold starts. Best for event-driven, spiky workloads.

**App Runner** — fully managed container platform. Push a Dockerfile or container image; AWS runs it, scales it, gives you HTTPS URL. Best for stateless web services without K8s overhead.

**Fargate** — serverless containers, runs as ECS tasks or EKS pods. You define container specs; AWS provisions and runs the underlying compute. No EC2 instances to manage.

**ECS on EC2** — ECS orchestrator with EC2 instances you manage. More cost control (Spot, Reserved Instances) but you handle node fleet, AMI updates, capacity planning.

**EKS** — managed Kubernetes; AWS runs the control plane; you (or Fargate) run the data plane. Standard K8s ecosystem, multi-cloud portability.

**EC2** — raw virtual machines; full OS control; you manage everything. The escape hatch when nothing else fits.

| Aspect | Lambda | App Runner | Fargate | ECS on EC2 | EKS | EC2 |

sections.title: Decision Tree by Workload Pattern
sections.content:
**Event-driven, short, spiky → Lambda**
- API Gateway endpoints with low and bursty RPS
- S3 event triggers (image processing on upload)
- SNS/SQS message processing (under 15 min per message)
- Scheduled tasks (EventBridge cron)
- Best when: cost matters and traffic is unpredictable; cold starts acceptable
- Anti-pattern: sustained 1000+ RPS production API — Lambda costs more than Fargate at that scale; use SnapStart for Java to mitigate cold starts but consider migration

**Stateless web service, no K8s needed → App Runner or Fargate**
- A Spring Boot service serving HTTPS at moderate RPS
- App Runner: simplest — push image, get URL; auto-scales by request volume
- Fargate: more control over VPC, networking, sidecars; works inside ECS
- Best when: you want zero node management; willing to pay slight premium over EC2

**Container fleet with cost optimization → ECS on EC2**
- Production containerized workload at scale where cost matters
- Mix On-Demand + Spot via capacity providers (50–80% cost savings)
- Use Graviton (ARM) instances for ~20% cheaper than x86 for ARM-compatible workloads
- Best when: scale is high enough that Fargate premium adds up; you have ops to manage AMI updates

**Multi-cloud or K8s ecosystem → EKS (with Fargate or EC2 nodes)**
- Want portability across clouds (the same manifests run on GKE, AKS, on-prem)
- Need K8s features: CRDs, Operators, advanced networking (service mesh), GitOps tooling
- Hybrid Fargate + EC2 nodes for cost optimization (Fargate for unpredictable, EC2 Spot for batch)
- Best when: you have K8s expertise and the ecosystem is worth the complexity
- Anti-pattern: 5-engineer startup adopting EKS for 3 services

**Full OS control or specialized hardware → EC2**
- GPU workloads (ML training/inference)
- HPC, specialized AMIs (FPGA, Inferentia)
- Software that doesn't containerize cleanly (Windows GUI, legacy systems)
- Long-running stateful workloads where you want to manage the OS
- Best when: containerization isn't viable or specialized hardware is needed

sections.title: Hidden Trade-offs and Cost Crossovers
sections.content:
**Lambda gets expensive at scale.** Lambda is incredibly cheap at low usage — millions of free invocations per month. But at sustained 1000+ RPS, the per-invocation cost adds up. Crossover with Fargate/ECS is around 30–50% utilization. A constantly-busy API on Lambda costs more than the same API on Fargate.

**Cold starts matter for Java more than other runtimes.** Java Lambda cold starts can be 1–3 seconds (JVM warmup). Mitigations: SnapStart (snapshots a warmed JVM, drops cold start to ~200ms), provisioned concurrency (always warm but you pay for idle), GraalVM native image (slower build, fast cold start). Node.js/Python cold starts are 100–300ms — less of a concern.

**Vendor lock-in is real.** Lambda code calls AWS SDK directly, uses AWS-specific event payloads, integrates tightly with API Gateway. Migrating away from Lambda means rewriting the dispatch layer. EKS is the most portable — same K8s manifests run on GKE, AKS, on-prem.

**Fargate has no Spot.** Fargate Spot exists but is less cost-effective than EC2 Spot. If you need Spot pricing (50–90% savings), ECS on EC2 or EKS with EC2 nodes win.

**EKS control plane cost.** $0.10/hr per cluster = $73/mo per cluster. With 20 clusters across regions = $1,460/mo just for control planes. At small scale this is significant; at large scale negligible.

**Graviton (ARM) for cost.** Graviton2/3/4 instances are 20–40% cheaper than x86 equivalents. JVM workloads work on ARM (build with ARM-compatible base images). Adoption is gating factor for cost optimization in 2026.

**App Runner has limits.** Designed for simple web services; lacks VPC features, complex routing, sidecar patterns. When you outgrow it, you migrate to Fargate. Don't pick App Runner for anything you might need to grow beyond a single container per service.

**Spot vs On-Demand vs Reserved.** Spot is 50–90% off but can be reclaimed in 2 minutes. Reserved is 30–70% off for 1–3 year commits. On-Demand is most expensive but most flexible. Mature production: mix all three based on workload tolerance for interruption.

**Compute Savings Plans** are easier than RIs — commit to $X/hr of compute spend; AWS applies it to Lambda, Fargate, or EC2 (any of them). Less operational overhead than juggling Reserved Instances per region/instance type.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Lambda** for event-driven, short, spiky workloads — cheapest at low usage; expensive at sustained high RPS; cold starts (especially Java) need mitigation
- **App Runner / Fargate** for stateless containers without managing servers — simplest path to running containers on AWS
- **ECS on EC2** when you want container orchestration with cost control via Spot, Reserved, and Graviton instances
- **EKS** when you need Kubernetes ecosystem — multi-cloud portability, CRDs/Operators, advanced features; highest operational complexity
- **EC2** when you need full OS control, specialized hardware, or workloads that don't containerize
- **Cost crossovers matter** — Lambda cheaper than Fargate at low utilization; Fargate easier than EC2 at low scale; EC2 cheaper at high scale with Spot/Reserved/Graviton
- **Vendor lock-in** is highest with Lambda, lowest with EKS — factor into long-term strategy

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
AWS gives you six main compute options. The choice depends on workload shape, your appetite for operational burden, and cost model. The spectrum runs from most-managed (Lambda) to most-control (EC2).

**Lambda — event-driven, spiky, short**
- You provide a function; AWS provides everything else — servers, scaling, patching
- Pay per invocation plus execution time; cheapest at low usage; gets expensive past sustained 1000+ RPS
- Limits: 15-minute max execution, 10GB memory, cold starts
- Java cold starts are the main pain — 1 to 3 seconds; mitigate with SnapStart (drops to ~200ms), provisioned concurrency (always warm but you pay for idle), or GraalVM native image
- Best for API Gateway endpoints with bursty traffic, S3 event triggers, scheduled tasks; not great for sustained high-RPS production APIs

**App Runner — stateless web services, simplest container option**
- Push a Dockerfile or image, AWS gives you an HTTPS URL with auto-scaling
- Lacks advanced features like VPC complexity, sidecars; outgrow it = migrate to Fargate

**Fargate — serverless containers**
- Containers running on ECS or EKS without managing the underlying EC2 instances
- Slight premium over EC2 but no node management; perfect when you want containers without K8s overhead
- Fargate Spot exists but is less cost-effective than EC2 Spot — if you need real Spot pricing, ECS on EC2 or EKS on EC2

**ECS on EC2 — cost-optimized container fleet**
- ECS orchestrator with EC2 instances you manage; capacity providers let you mix On-Demand and Spot
- Spot saves 50 to 90 percent for interruption-tolerant workloads; Graviton (ARM) instances 20 to 40 percent cheaper than x86
- Best when scale is high enough that the Fargate premium adds up

**EKS — Kubernetes ecosystem, multi-cloud portability**
- AWS-managed control plane at $0.10 per hour per cluster ($73 per month); you (or Fargate) run the data plane
- Standard K8s manifests run on GKE, AKS, on-prem — the portability story
- Best when you need K8s features (CRDs, Operators, service mesh) and have the ops to manage the complexity
- Anti-pattern: 5-engineer startup adopting EKS for 3 services; over-engineering

**EC2 — raw VMs, full control**
- The escape hatch — GPU workloads for ML, HPC, specialized hardware (FPGA, Inferentia), Windows GUI, software that doesn't containerize cleanly
- You manage everything — OS patches, AMIs, scaling, monitoring

**The cost crossovers everyone misses**
- Lambda is cheaper than Fargate at low utilization; the crossover is around 30 to 50 percent sustained utilization
- Fargate is easier than EC2 at low scale; EC2 wins on cost at high scale with Spot, Reserved, and Graviton
- EKS control plane at $73 per month per cluster — negligible at scale, significant for many small clusters

**Vendor lock-in is real**
- Lambda is the most locked-in — code calls AWS SDK directly, uses AWS-specific event payloads, integrates tightly with API Gateway; migration means rewriting dispatch
- EKS is the most portable — same K8s manifests run anywhere; the open-source standard
- Factor lock-in into long-term strategy alongside cost and ops burden

**Default recommendation by stage**
- Startup with bursty workloads: Lambda + App Runner; minimal ops, pay only when used
- Mid-size with steady workloads: Fargate or ECS on EC2; balance cost and ops
- Mature org with K8s expertise and multi-cloud goals: EKS
- Specialized needs: EC2 with the right instance type

questions.question: RDS vs Aurora vs DynamoDB — which AWS database and when?
questions.title: AWS Database Comparison: RDS vs Aurora vs DynamoDB
questions.direct_answer: **RDS** for standard relational workloads — managed Postgres/MySQL/MariaDB; familiar, portable, predictable cost. **Aurora** for relational workloads at scale — 5x throughput of RDS, 6-way replicated storage, faster failover; AWS-specific. **DynamoDB** for high-scale key-value/document workloads where you can design around its access patterns — single-digit ms, infinite scale, but no joins/transactions across partitions. Default to RDS; reach for Aurora at scale; pick DynamoDB when access patterns are well-defined and scale is huge.

sections.title: Three Databases for Three Different Patterns
sections.content:
AWS's main database options solve different problems. The choice usually comes down to: do you need relational with joins/transactions, or do you have well-defined access patterns at huge scale?

**RDS** (Relational Database Service) is managed Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, or SQL Server. AWS handles backups, patching, multi-AZ failover, point-in-time restore. You get the same database engine you'd run yourself, just managed. Best for standard relational workloads up to a few hundred GB and moderate traffic.

**Aurora** is AWS's reimplementation of MySQL/PostgreSQL with a custom storage layer. The compute is MySQL/Postgres-compatible (existing apps work unchanged), but the storage is replicated 6 ways across 3 AZs and decoupled from compute. Result: 5x throughput of RDS MySQL, faster failover (~30s vs minutes for RDS), faster recovery, better at large scale (up to 128TB). Trade-off: AWS-specific, slightly more expensive at low scale.

**DynamoDB** is a fully managed NoSQL key-value/document database. Single-digit millisecond latency at any scale (tested at trillions of requests/day at Amazon retail). On-demand or provisioned capacity. The catch: you must design around access patterns at the start — it lacks joins, has limited query flexibility, and ad-hoc queries are expensive. Single-table design is the canonical pattern.

There are also: **DocumentDB** (MongoDB-compatible managed NoSQL), **Neptune** (graph), **Keyspaces** (Cassandra-compatible), **Timestream** (time-series), **OpenSearch** (search/analytics), and **Redshift** (data warehouse) — each for specific niches.

sections.title: Feature-by-Feature Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | RDS | Aurora | DynamoDB |
|--------|-----|--------|----------|
| **Type** | Relational | Relational | NoSQL key-value/document |
| **Engines** | Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server | MySQL, Postgres-compatible | DynamoDB (proprietary) |
| **Max storage** | 64TB | 128TB | Unlimited |
| **Throughput** | Tied to instance | 5x RDS MySQL | Unlimited (per partition limits) |
| **Replication** | Async read replicas | 6-way replicated storage | 3-way replicated automatically |
| **Failover time** | 60–120s (multi-AZ) | ~30s | Instant (no concept) |
| **Scaling** | Vertical (instance size) + read replicas | Vertical + horizontal readers (up to 15) | Auto-scaled, partition-based |
| **Joins / SQL** | Full SQL | Full SQL | None (single-table design or PartiQL with limits) |
| **Transactions** | Full ACID | Full ACID | Limited (1MB / 100 items per txn, single-region) |
| **Pricing model** | Per instance-hour + storage | Per instance-hour + storage | On-demand (per request) or provisioned (RCU/WCU) |
| **Vendor lock-in** | Low (portable Postgres/MySQL) | Medium (Aurora-specific features) | High (proprietary) |
| **Best for** | Standard relational workloads | Relational at scale, faster failover | High-scale key-value, well-defined access patterns |
| **Examples** | Most Spring apps | High-traffic SaaS, multi-region | Amazon retail, gaming, IoT |

sections.title: Decision Tree by Workload
sections.content:
**Pick RDS Postgres/MySQL when:**
- Standard relational workload up to ~64TB
- Moderate traffic (a few thousand QPS for primary)
- Want maximum portability — same Postgres/MySQL runs on-prem, on GCP, on Azure
- Cost-sensitive at small scale (RDS is cheaper than Aurora at low usage)
- Examples: most Spring/Django/Rails web apps; internal tools

**Pick Aurora MySQL/Postgres when:**
- High traffic relational workload (10k+ QPS or large data volume)
- Need fast failover — 30s vs 60–120s for RDS multi-AZ
- Want up to 15 read replicas (RDS caps lower)
- Need read scaling beyond what RDS replicas provide
- Multi-region active-passive (Aurora Global Database)
- Variable traffic with spikes — Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute up/down by ACU
- Examples: high-traffic SaaS, large e-commerce, fintech

**Pick DynamoDB when:**
- Access patterns are well-defined and won't change much
- Need single-digit ms latency at any scale (millions of QPS)
- Workload is key-value or document, not relational
- Traffic is unpredictable (on-demand pricing scales perfectly)
- Examples: shopping cart, session store, IoT telemetry, gaming leaderboards, real-time bidding

**Anti-pattern**: picking DynamoDB because "it scales" without designing access patterns first. DynamoDB's single-table design requires upfront thinking about every query you'll need. Adding a new query pattern to an existing table requires a global secondary index (GSI) or a redesign — both expensive. RDBMS is much more forgiving to evolving requirements.

**Pick a specialized DB when:**
- **Cassandra-compatible scale**: Keyspaces
- **MongoDB API**: DocumentDB (caveat: not all MongoDB features supported)
- **Graph queries**: Neptune (relationships, recommendations)
- **Time-series**: Timestream (sensor data, monitoring)
- **Search/analytics**: OpenSearch
- **Data warehouse**: Redshift

**The default**: start with RDS Postgres for new projects; migrate to Aurora when scale demands it; reserve DynamoDB for specific high-scale use cases where access patterns are clear.

sections.title: Hidden Trade-offs and Common Pitfalls
sections.content:
**RDS multi-AZ failover is slower than people expect.** The standby is exactly that — a standby; failover is 60–120 seconds typically. For HA SLOs under 99.99%, RDS is fine. For tighter SLOs, Aurora's ~30s is materially better.

**Aurora Serverless v2 changes the equation.** Aurora used to require sizing instances; Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute by ACU (Aurora Capacity Units) in seconds based on load. For variable workloads, it can be cheaper than provisioned. v1 was different and limited — don't confuse them.

**Aurora I/O-Optimized vs Standard.** Standard Aurora charges per I/O; for I/O-heavy workloads, this gets expensive fast. I/O-Optimized has no per-I/O charge but higher base instance cost — crossover around 25% I/O-spend ratio. Pick based on workload; switch via console if needed.

**DynamoDB single-table design is non-obvious.** The mental model from RDBMS doesn't apply. You design one table with composite keys (PK + SK) that satisfy multiple query patterns simultaneously. Read DynamoDB Book by Alex DeBrie before starting. Multi-table design is acceptable for simple cases but doesn't scale to complex apps.

**DynamoDB hot partitions.** A partition gets 1000 WCU / 3000 RCU max; a hot partition (one popular hash key) throttles. Adaptive capacity helps but doesn't eliminate the issue. Design partition keys with high cardinality (user_id, not country).

**DynamoDB Global Tables for multi-region.** Bidirectional replication across regions; eventual consistency between regions. Useful for global apps but conflict resolution is last-writer-wins per attribute — may not match your semantic.

**Backup costs.** All three offer automated backups, but for large databases, backup storage cost adds up. Aurora's continuous backup approach is more efficient than RDS snapshots.

**RDS Proxy reduces connection storms.** Java apps with HikariCP creating thousands of connections during scaling events overwhelm RDS. RDS Proxy multiplexes connections — critical for Lambda + RDS architectures. Aurora doesn't need it as much (built-in connection management).

**Don't forget Aurora's 6-way storage replication.** A single Aurora cluster's storage is replicated across 3 AZs, 2 copies per AZ. AZ-level failures are transparent. RDS multi-AZ has 2 copies (one per AZ) — lower durability.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **RDS** for standard relational workloads — portable, familiar, cost-effective at small/medium scale; failover takes 60–120s
- **Aurora** for relational at scale — 5x throughput, ~30s failover, 6-way replicated storage, up to 15 read replicas; AWS-specific
- **DynamoDB** for high-scale key-value workloads where access patterns are well-defined upfront — single-digit ms, no joins, single-table design pattern
- **Aurora Serverless v2** scales compute by ACU in seconds — great for variable workloads; cheaper than provisioned for spiky traffic
- **DynamoDB hot partitions** — design partition keys with high cardinality; user_id, not country
- **RDS Proxy** for connection-heavy architectures (especially Lambda + RDS) to avoid connection storms
- **Default**: RDS Postgres → Aurora at scale → DynamoDB only when access patterns are clear and scale demands it

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
AWS database choice usually comes down to: do you need relational with joins and transactions, or do you have well-defined access patterns at huge scale that justify the trade-offs of NoSQL.

**RDS — the standard managed relational**
- Managed Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, or SQL Server; AWS handles backups, patching, multi-AZ failover
- Same database engine you'd run yourself, just managed; maximum portability across clouds and on-prem
- Best for standard relational workloads up to 64TB and moderate traffic; the default for most Spring apps
- Failover takes 60 to 120 seconds in multi-AZ — fine for 99.9% SLOs but not for tighter

**Aurora — AWS's reimplementation of MySQL and Postgres**
- Compute is MySQL or Postgres compatible — existing apps work unchanged
- Storage is the magic: 6-way replicated across 3 AZs, decoupled from compute
- 5x throughput of RDS MySQL, ~30 second failover, up to 15 read replicas, supports up to 128TB
- Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute by ACU in seconds — cheaper than provisioned for variable traffic
- Trade-off: AWS-specific (some lock-in), slightly more expensive at low scale

**DynamoDB — fully managed NoSQL**
- Single-digit millisecond latency at any scale; tested at trillions of requests per day at Amazon retail
- On-demand pricing scales perfectly with unpredictable traffic; provisioned mode for steady predictable workloads
- The catch: you must design around access patterns at the start — single-table design is the canonical pattern
- Lacks joins; limited query flexibility; ad-hoc queries are expensive or require GSIs (global secondary indexes)

**The decision tree**
- Standard web app, predictable scale: RDS Postgres — the default
- High-traffic relational, faster failover, more read replicas: Aurora
- Key-value or document workload at huge scale with well-defined queries: DynamoDB
- Specialized: DocumentDB for MongoDB API, Neptune for graphs, Keyspaces for Cassandra, Timestream for time-series, OpenSearch for search

**The classic anti-pattern**
- Picking DynamoDB because "it scales" without designing access patterns first
- Single-table design requires upfront thinking about every query you'll need; adding a new query pattern later requires a GSI or table redesign
- RDBMS is much more forgiving to evolving requirements

**Hidden trade-offs to call out**
- RDS multi-AZ failover is slower than people expect (60 to 120 seconds); Aurora's 30 seconds is materially better for tight SLOs
- Aurora I/O-Optimized vs Standard — I/O-heavy workloads get expensive on Standard; crossover around 25 percent I/O-spend ratio; switch via console
- DynamoDB hot partitions — 1000 WCU / 3000 RCU max per partition; design partition keys with high cardinality (user_id, not country)
- Aurora's 6-way replicated storage is more durable than RDS multi-AZ's 2 copies
- RDS Proxy is critical for Lambda + RDS to avoid connection storms; multiplexes connections

**Default recommendation**
- Start new projects on RDS Postgres for relational — portable, familiar, cheap
- Migrate to Aurora when scale or failover SLO demands it
- Reserve DynamoDB for specific high-scale use cases where access patterns are clear and won't change much
- For specialized needs (graph, time-series, search), use the purpose-built services rather than forcing them into a relational or DynamoDB model

questions.question: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge vs Kinesis vs MSK — which AWS messaging service?
questions.title: AWS Messaging Compared: SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis, MSK
questions.direct_answer: **SQS** for point-to-point queues with one consumer per message — worker pulls from queue, processes, deletes. **SNS** for fan-out to multiple subscribers — one publish, many destinations. **EventBridge** for event-driven architectures with content-based routing — publish events, rules route to targets based on JSON pattern matching. **Kinesis Data Streams** for high-throughput ordered streaming with replay (clickstream, logs). **MSK** (managed Kafka) when you need Kafka semantics specifically (multi-cloud, ecosystem, exactly-once).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical messaging architecture choice across patterns and scale
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using SNS → SQS fan-out when EventBridge with rules is simpler; or using Kinesis when SQS would suffice
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss FIFO vs Standard SQS, EventBridge schema registry, Kinesis shard design, and MSK vs Kinesis (Kafka ecosystem vs serverless)

sections.title: Five Messaging Services for Five Distinct Patterns
sections.content:
AWS has multiple messaging services because there's no one-size-fits-all messaging primitive. Each fits a specific pattern.

**SQS (Simple Queue Service)** — point-to-point queue. Producer sends messages; one consumer pulls and processes each message; once acknowledged (DeleteMessage), it's gone. Use cases: background job processing, decoupling services, buffering bursts. Two flavors: Standard (high throughput, at-least-once, no order guarantee) and FIFO (ordered, exactly-once-ish, lower throughput).

**SNS (Simple Notification Service)** — pub/sub fan-out. Publisher sends one message; SNS delivers to N subscribers (SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP endpoints, email/SMS). Subscribers don't know about publishers. Use cases: notifying multiple downstream services of an event.

**EventBridge** — event bus with content-based routing. Publishers send events; rules match events by JSON patterns and route to targets (Lambda, Step Functions, SQS, SNS, third-party SaaS). Replaces the SNS → SQS fan-out pattern with smarter routing. Schema registry tracks event shapes. Use cases: modern event-driven architectures, SaaS integrations.

**Kinesis Data Streams** — ordered stream of records partitioned by shard. Multiple consumers can read independently with their own checkpoints (replay capability). Records persist 24h–1yr. Use cases: clickstream, log aggregation, real-time analytics, IoT telemetry.

**MSK (Managed Streaming for Kafka)** — managed Apache Kafka. Same Kafka API, AWS handles brokers, ZooKeeper/KRaft, patches. Use when you need Kafka specifically: multi-cloud portability, Kafka ecosystem (Connect, Streams, ksqlDB), exactly-once semantics, or existing Kafka skills.

A sixth: **MQ** (managed ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ) for legacy AMQP/STOMP/MQTT — use when migrating off existing brokers.

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | SQS | SNS | EventBridge | Kinesis | MSK (Kafka) |
|--------|-----|-----|-------------|---------|-------------|
| **Pattern** | Point-to-point queue | Fan-out pub/sub | Event bus + rules | Ordered stream | Distributed log |
| **Delivery model** | One consumer per message | All subscribers get message | Routed by rule pattern | Multiple consumers, own offset | Multiple consumers, own offset |
| **Order** | FIFO option (5K msg/s/group) | Per-publish | Best-effort | Per-shard | Per-partition |
| **Throughput** | Standard: unlimited; FIFO: 30K msg/s | Unlimited | 2400 events/s default (raisable) | Per-shard limit (1MB/s in, 2MB/s out) | High (Kafka) |
| **Persistence** | 14 days max | None (ephemeral routing) | None (ephemeral routing) | 24h–1yr | Configurable, days/forever |
| **Replay** | No | No | Archive + replay | Yes (via checkpoint) | Yes |
| **Pricing** | Per million requests | Per million requests | Per million events | Per shard-hour + per put | Per broker-hour |
| **Best for** | Background jobs, buffering | Notifying multiple endpoints | Event-driven architecture | Streams, analytics, IoT | Kafka ecosystem, multi-cloud |
| **Common mistake** | Using when you need order (Standard not FIFO) | Using SNS→SQS when EventBridge fits | Misunderstanding rule patterns (no aggregation) | Picking when SQS would suffice | Using when MSK overhead unjustified |

sections.title: Decision Tree by Pattern
sections.content:
**Use SQS when:**
- One worker should process each message exactly once (or at-least-once, with idempotency)
- Background jobs from a web tier (decouple async processing)
- Buffering bursts (web tier writes to queue, workers process at sustainable rate)
- Scheduled fan-in (multiple producers, single queue, workers pull)

FIFO when order matters (per message group); Standard otherwise (much higher throughput).

**Use SNS when:**
- Need to notify multiple downstream services of one event
- Email/SMS/push notifications to end users
- Publish to multiple SQS queues from one event (classic SNS → SQS fan-out)
- Note: EventBridge often better for service-to-service fan-out (filtering)

**Use EventBridge when:**
- Modern event-driven architecture with multiple producers and consumers
- Need to route events based on content (JSON pattern matching)
- Integrating with SaaS (Auth0, PagerDuty, Datadog — EventBridge has SaaS partner sources)
- Schema registry for event contracts (good practice for cross-team events)
- Cross-account / cross-region event distribution

**Use Kinesis Data Streams when:**
- Ordered processing of a high-volume stream
- Multiple consumers each maintaining their own position (checkpoint)
- Replay capability needed (re-process from a specific point)
- Real-time analytics, clickstream, log aggregation, IoT telemetry
- Use Firehose if you just need to land in S3/Redshift/OpenSearch

**Use MSK when:**
- You specifically need Kafka API (existing apps, multi-cloud, ecosystem)
- Need Kafka Connect, Kafka Streams, ksqlDB
- Need exactly-once semantics with transactions across topics
- Higher throughput than Kinesis at lower cost (at scale)
- Have Kafka expertise on the team

**Use MQ when:**
- Migrating from on-prem ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ
- Need AMQP, STOMP, MQTT, OpenWire protocols
- Don't pick for new projects unless protocol-locked

**The default**: SQS for queues, SNS for simple fan-out, EventBridge for modern event-driven, Kinesis for streams. MSK only when Kafka-specific features are needed.

sections.title: Hidden Trade-offs and Pitfalls
sections.content:
**SQS Standard vs FIFO trade-off.** Standard is unlimited throughput but at-least-once and unordered; FIFO is ordered + exactly-once-ish but capped at 30K msg/s with batching. Pick based on whether duplicates and reorders are tolerable.

**SQS visibility timeout vs processing time.** When a message is pulled, it's invisible for the visibility timeout (default 30s). If processing takes longer, the message reappears and another worker picks it up — duplicate processing. Set visibility timeout > worst-case processing time, or use ChangeMessageVisibility heartbeat for long jobs.

**SNS → SQS fan-out is the legacy pattern.** EventBridge with SQS targets does the same with content-based filtering. Use EventBridge for new event-driven systems; SNS for simple notification (no filtering needed).

**EventBridge rule limits.** 300 rules per bus default (raisable). Each rule can have up to 5 targets. Complex routing across hundreds of event types may hit limits.

**EventBridge no aggregation.** Rules match events but don't aggregate — you can't say "trigger after 100 events." Use Kinesis or Step Functions for aggregation.

**Kinesis shard limits and resharding.** Each shard: 1MB/s write, 2MB/s read, 1000 records/s. Hot partition (one shard receiving most data) bottlenecks. Resharding is operational pain; use random partition keys when ordering doesn't matter at the partition level.

**Kinesis vs MSK at scale.** Kinesis is serverless and simpler; MSK gives true Kafka with better economics at huge scale (millions of events/s). MSK Serverless reduces ops but costs more than provisioned MSK at high scale.

**Kinesis Firehose vs Streams.** Firehose lands data in destinations (S3, Redshift, OpenSearch) with no consumer code. Streams require consumers (KCL or Lambda). Use Firehose if you just need to write to a destination; Streams when you need real-time custom processing.

**Cost surprises.** SNS pricing per delivery (not per publish) — fan-out to 1000 subscribers is 1000 charged deliveries. EventBridge per event published. Kinesis charges per shard-hour even when idle. Lambda + Kinesis adds GetRecords charges. Model cost before committing.

**Dead-letter queues are mandatory.** All these services need DLQs (or DLT in EventBridge) for unprocessable messages — otherwise you lose them or block the queue forever. Configure DLQ from day one.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **SQS** for point-to-point queues — background jobs, buffering bursts; FIFO for ordered, Standard for high throughput
- **SNS** for fan-out pub/sub — one publish to many subscribers; legacy pattern is SNS → SQS, EventBridge often better today
- **EventBridge** for modern event-driven architecture — content-based routing via JSON patterns, schema registry, SaaS integrations
- **Kinesis Data Streams** for ordered streams with multiple consumers and replay — clickstream, IoT, real-time analytics
- **MSK** when you need Kafka specifically — ecosystem (Connect, Streams), exactly-once, multi-cloud portability
- **DLQs are mandatory** — configure from day one to handle unprocessable messages
- **Cost modeling matters** — SNS per delivery, EventBridge per event, Kinesis per shard-hour; small choices compound at scale

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
AWS has multiple messaging services because there's no one-size-fits-all messaging primitive. Each fits a specific pattern.

**SQS — point-to-point queue**
- Producer sends messages; one consumer pulls and processes each; once acknowledged with DeleteMessage, it's gone
- Two flavors: Standard (unlimited throughput, at-least-once, no order) and FIFO (ordered, exactly-once-ish, capped at 30K messages per second)
- Use for background job processing, buffering bursts, decoupling services
- The visibility timeout trap: when a message is pulled it's invisible for the timeout (default 30 seconds); if processing exceeds that, the message reappears and another worker picks it up — duplicates; use heartbeat or longer timeout

**SNS — fan-out pub/sub**
- Publisher sends one message; SNS delivers to N subscribers (SQS queues, Lambda, HTTP endpoints, email, SMS)
- Subscribers don't know about publishers; classic for notifying multiple downstream services
- The legacy pattern: SNS → SQS for fan-out to multiple queues; EventBridge often better today because of filtering

**EventBridge — event bus with content-based routing**
- Publishers send events; rules match events by JSON patterns and route to targets (Lambda, Step Functions, SQS, SNS, third-party SaaS)
- Schema registry tracks event shapes — good practice for cross-team event contracts
- The modern default for event-driven architecture; replaces SNS → SQS fan-out with smarter content-based routing
- Limitation: rules match individual events; no aggregation (use Kinesis or Step Functions if you need "trigger after N events")

**Kinesis Data Streams — ordered stream with replay**
- Records partitioned by shard; multiple consumers can each maintain their own offset/checkpoint
- Records persist 24 hours up to 1 year, enabling replay from a specific point
- Use for clickstream, log aggregation, real-time analytics, IoT telemetry
- Shard limits: 1MB/s write, 2MB/s read, 1000 records/s per shard; hot partition is bottleneck; design partition keys carefully

**MSK — managed Kafka**
- Same Kafka API, AWS handles brokers, ZooKeeper or KRaft, patches
- Use when you need Kafka specifically: ecosystem (Connect, Streams, ksqlDB), exactly-once with transactions, multi-cloud portability, existing Kafka skills
- Higher operational complexity than Kinesis but better economics at huge scale and richer feature set

**The decision tree**
- Background jobs, queue pattern, one consumer per message: SQS
- Notify multiple destinations of one event with no filtering: SNS
- Modern event-driven architecture with content-based routing: EventBridge
- Ordered stream with multiple consumers and replay: Kinesis
- Need Kafka API specifically: MSK
- Migrating from on-prem ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ: MQ (otherwise don't pick)

**Hidden trade-offs**
- SNS pricing is per delivery, not per publish — fan-out to 1000 subscribers is 1000 charged deliveries
- EventBridge has 300 rules per bus default; complex routing across hundreds of event types may hit limits
- Kinesis charges per shard-hour even when idle; over-provisioning gets expensive
- Kinesis Firehose vs Streams — Firehose lands data in S3/Redshift/OpenSearch with no consumer code; Streams needs consumers but allows custom real-time processing
- DLQs are mandatory across all of these — configure from day one to handle unprocessable messages, otherwise you lose them or block forever

**Default recommendation**
- New event-driven architecture: EventBridge as the bus, SQS for work queues, Lambda or ECS as targets
- Stream processing: Kinesis Data Streams for AWS-native, MSK if you specifically need Kafka
- Avoid: SNS → SQS fan-out for new projects (use EventBridge), MQ (legacy migration only)
